_comment: Detection rules for loganalyzer. Edit thresholds here; no code change needed. Each rule has: id, name, type (detector), severity (low|medium|high|critical), sources, params (thresholds/patterns), mitre mapping, recommended response.

rules.name: Brute-force login attempts from one source
rules.description: One source IP produced many failed logins in a short window with several attempts per account, the classic pattern of automated password guessing (SSH, RDP/SMB on Windows). Bursts that touch many accounts only once or twice are reported as password spraying (AUTH-002) instead.
response: Block or rate-limit the source IP at the firewall / fail2ban / Windows Firewall.
Check whether any login from this IP succeeded (see AUTH-003) and review the targeted accounts.
Confirm SSH password authentication is disabled where possible (keys only) and that account lockout is configured on Windows.
Add the IP to the incident ticket and check threat-intel / abuse reports before closing.

rules.name: Password spraying: many accounts, few tries each
rules.description: One source IP tried a few passwords against many different usernames. Spraying stays under per-account lockout thresholds, so it is detected by counting distinct accounts instead of failures per account.
response: Block the source IP and notify the identity/security owner.
Force a password reset and review sign-in history for every account that was targeted, starting with any that later succeeded.
Check for weak or reused passwords against a banned-password list; enable MFA for remote access.
Look for the same IP in web and VPN logs.

rules.name: Successful login after many failures
rules.description: A source IP that had just generated many failed logins then logged in successfully. This is the strongest sign that a brute-force or spraying attempt actually worked.
response: Treat the account as compromised: disable it or force a password reset and revoke active sessions/keys immediately.
Isolate the host if possible and preserve logs (copy auth.log / Security.evtx) before making changes.
Review everything the account did after the successful login: new users, sudo/admin use, new processes, outbound connections.
Escalate to the security lead / incident owner.

rules.name: New local account created
rules.description: A new user account was created (Windows event 4720 or Linux useradd). Legitimate during onboarding, but attackers create accounts to keep access.
response: Verify there is an approved ticket/change request for the account and who created it.
If unexpected, disable the account and review who/what created it.
Check group memberships of the new account (see ACCT-002).

rules.name: New account given administrative rights
rules.description: A newly created account was added to an administrative group (Windows 4732 Administrators, Linux sudo/wheel) or used special privileges (4672) shortly after creation, a typical persistence step after gaining access.
response: Disable the new account and remove it from privileged groups right away.
Identify the session that created it (creator account, source IP, time) and treat that account as compromised.
Search the host for scheduled tasks, services, SSH keys and startup items added around the same time.
Escalate as a security incident; do not delete the account until evidence is captured.

rules.name: Successful login outside business hours
rules.description: A successful interactive or remote login happened outside configured business hours (07:00-19:00 Mon-Fri). Severity rises when special privileges were assigned to the same user (event 4672). Alone this is a weak signal: confirm with the user before escalating.
response: Contact the user (by a known phone number or chat, not by replying to anything suspicious) to confirm the login was theirs.
If unconfirmed, reset the password, revoke sessions and review the activity during that session.
Check whether the source IP/location is normal for this user (VPN range, usual country).

rules.name: HTTP 404 flood (content/directory scanning)
rules.description: One client generated a large number of 404 responses in a short time, typical of directory brute-forcing and automated vulnerability scanners.
response: Rate-limit or block the client at the WAF / reverse proxy.
Check whether any request from this IP returned 200 for a sensitive path (admin pages, backups, .env, .git).
Make sure nothing sensitive is exposed on the web root; keep the scan results for the ticket.

rules.name: SQL injection probes
rules.description: Requests contain SQL injection payloads (UNION SELECT, boolean/time-based tests, information_schema). Severity is raised to critical if any such request produced an HTTP 500, which can mean a payload reached the database layer and caused an error.
response: Block the source IP at the WAF and review application/database logs for the same time window.
For requests that returned 500, hand to the developers to check whether the endpoint uses parameterised queries and what the application error log says.
Check database logs for unusual queries or large result sets; rotate credentials if data exposure is suspected.

rules.name: Cross-site scripting (XSS) probes
rules.description: Requests contain script injection payloads (<script>, onerror=, javascript:). These are usually automated tests for reflected XSS.
response: Block or rate-limit the source IP.
Ask the web team to confirm the targeted parameters are output-encoded and a Content-Security-Policy is set.
Search logs for the same payloads from other IPs.

rules.name: Path traversal / local file inclusion probes
rules.description: Requests try to escape the web root using ../ sequences or request OS files such as /etc/passwd. A 200 response to such a request is escalated to critical because the file may have been served.
response: Block the source IP at the WAF.
For any 200 response, check what was returned (response size in the log) and inspect the application for unsafe file path handling; treat as a data exposure until disproved.
Update the web server / framework and confirm the web process runs with least privilege.

rules.name: Probing for sensitive files and admin panels
rules.description: A client requested several well-known sensitive or admin paths (.env, .git, phpMyAdmin, wp-login). Commonly seen from opportunistic scanners looking for exposed secrets.
response: Confirm none of these paths exist or are reachable from the internet.
Block or rate-limit the client.
Rotate any secret that could have lived in an exposed file.

rules.name: Known scanner / attack-tool user agent
rules.description: The User-Agent header names a well-known scanning or exploitation tool. User agents are trivially spoofed, so absence of this alert proves nothing, but presence is a reliable sign of unauthorised scanning.
response: Block the client and check what else it requested (see WEB-001..WEB-005 alerts for the same IP).
If this is your own authorised scan, add it to the allow-list and record the approval.

rules.name: Scripted or empty user agent with high request volume
rules.description: A script-style or blank user agent made many requests. Often benign (monitoring, scrapers, integrations) but worth a look when combined with other alerts.
response: Check what the client requested; if it only fetches public pages, consider rate-limiting.
Correlate with other alerts from the same IP before taking action.

rules.name: Encoded PowerShell command
rules.description: A process was started with PowerShell -EncodedCommand and a long Base64 blob (event 4688 with command-line auditing). Used to hide the real command from casual inspection.
response: Decode the Base64 payload (UTF-16LE) on an isolated machine to see what it does.
Identify the parent process and user; isolate the host if the payload is malicious.
Check for follow-on activity: downloads, new accounts, scheduled tasks.

rules.name: Command-line file download (living off the land)
rules.description: Built-in tools (certutil, bitsadmin, PowerShell web cmdlets) were used to download a file, a common way to fetch malware without dropping an obvious downloader.
response: Find the URL and the file written; check reputation and quarantine the file.
Isolate the host if the download is not expected software deployment.
Review the parent process and the logged-on user for compromise.

rules.name: Account added via net.exe
rules.description: net.exe was used to create a user or add one to the local Administrators group from the command line.
response: Verify with the change record and the user who ran it; disable the new account if unexpected.
Review the account's logins and group membership, and the session that created it.

rules.name: Post-compromise reconnaissance commands
rules.description: Several discovery commands (whoami /all, net group, nltest, systeminfo) ran on the same host by the same user. Individually normal for admins; as a burst they look like an attacker orienting themselves.
response: Ask the user/admin whether they ran these commands; if not, treat the session as hostile.
Check what happened immediately before and after on the host (logons, new processes).

rules.name: Shadow copy / recovery inhibition
rules.description: Commands that delete volume shadow copies or disable Windows recovery, a hallmark of ransomware preparation.
response: Isolate the host from the network immediately.
Escalate to the incident lead; do not reboot until memory/disk evidence is captured.
Verify the state of backups and check other hosts for the same command.
